name: Divisibility and Congruences
description: Gcd, modular arithmetic and the classical theorems built on them.

content.answer: For integers $a$ and $b > 0$ there are unique $q, r$ with $a = bq + r$ and $0 \le r < b$.
acceptableAnswers: For integers a and b > 0 there are unique q, r with a = bq + r and 0 ≤ r < b.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: $\gcd(a,b) = ax + by$ for some integers $x, y$.
acceptableAnswers: gcd(a,b) = ax + by for some integers x, y.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: Repeatedly replace $(a,b)$ with $(b, a \bmod b)$; the last nonzero remainder is $\gcd(a,b)$.
acceptableAnswers: Repeatedly replace (a,b) with (b, a mod b); the last nonzero remainder is gcd(a,b).

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: $a \cdot b$ (for positive $a, b$)
acceptableAnswers: a · b (for positive a, b)

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: If a prime $p$ divides $ab$, then $p$ divides $a$ or $p$ divides $b$.
acceptableAnswers: If a prime p divides ab, then p divides a or p divides b.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: Every integer $> 1$ factors into primes uniquely up to order.
acceptableAnswers: Every integer > 1 factors into primes uniquely up to order.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: $n$ divides $(a - b)$.
acceptableAnswers: n divides (a - b).

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

cards.prompt: Linear congruence $ax \equiv b \pmod{n}$ has a solution iff

content.answer: $\gcd(a,n)$ divides $b$.
acceptableAnswers: gcd(a,n) divides b.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

acceptableAnswers: gcd(a,n) = 1.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: If the moduli $n_1, \ldots, n_k$ are pairwise coprime, the system $x \equiv a_i \pmod{n_i}$ has a unique solution mod $n_1 \cdots n_k$.
acceptableAnswers: If the moduli n1..nk are pairwise coprime, the system x ≡ ai (mod ni) has a unique solution mod n1···nk.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: If $p$ is prime and $p \nmid a$, then $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$.
acceptableAnswers: If p is prime and p ∤ a, then a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p).

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: If $\gcd(a,n) = 1$, then $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$.
acceptableAnswers: If gcd(a,n) = 1, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n).

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: The count of integers in $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ that are coprime to $n$.
acceptableAnswers: The count of integers in 1..n that are coprime to n.

content.answer: $\varphi(m)\,\varphi(n)$
acceptableAnswers: φ(m) φ(n)

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: An integer $p > 1$ is prime iff $(p - 1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$.
acceptableAnswers: An integer p > 1 is prime iff (p - 1)! ≡ -1 (mod p).

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

cards.prompt: Number of positive divisors of $n = p_1^{a_1} \cdots p_k^{a_k}$
cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)
Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: The digit sum is divisible by 3 (or by 9).

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: The alternating sum of the digits is divisible by 11.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: The least $k > 0$ with $a^k \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$; it divides $\varphi(n)$.
acceptableAnswers: The least k > 0 with a^k ≡ 1 (mod n); it divides φ(n).

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: An element whose order is $\varphi(n)$; it generates all units mod $n$.
acceptableAnswers: An element whose order is φ(n); it generates all units mod n.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: 1, 2, 4, $p^k$, and $2p^k$ for odd primes $p$.
acceptableAnswers: 1, 2, 4, p^k, and 2p^k for odd primes p.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: An $a$ not divisible by $p$ for which $x^2 \equiv a \pmod{p}$ has a solution.
acceptableAnswers: An a not divisible by p for which x^2 ≡ a (mod p) has a solution.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: $a$ is a quadratic residue mod $p$ iff $a^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$.
acceptableAnswers: a is a quadratic residue mod p iff a^((p-1)/2) ≡ 1 (mod p).

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)\left(\frac{q}{p}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \cdot \frac{q-1}{2}}$

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

cards.prompt: Which primes are sums of two squares (Fermat)?

content.answer: 2 and the primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$.
acceptableAnswers: 2 and the primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4).

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: Every positive integer is a sum of four integer squares.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: Given primes $p_1, \ldots, p_k$, any prime factor of $p_1 \cdots p_k + 1$ is a new prime.
acceptableAnswers: Given primes p1..pk, any prime factor of p1···pk + 1 is a new prime.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

cards.prompt: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions

content.answer: If $\gcd(a,d) = 1$, then $a, a+d, a+2d, \ldots$ contains infinitely many primes.
acceptableAnswers: If gcd(a,d) = 1, then a, a+d, a+2d, ... contains infinitely many primes.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: The number of primes $\le x$ is asymptotic to $\frac{x}{\ln x}$.
acceptableAnswers: The number of primes ≤ x is asymptotic to x / ln x.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: For every $n > 1$ there is a prime $p$ with $n < p < 2n$.
acceptableAnswers: For every n > 1 there is a prime p with n < p < 2n.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: $(m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2)$ with $m > n$, coprime, opposite parity.
acceptableAnswers: (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2) with m > n, coprime, opposite parity.

cards.sourceRef: Niven, Zuckerman & Montgomery, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (Wiley)

content.answer: $x^n + y^n = z^n$ has no positive-integer solutions for $n > 2$ (proved by Wiles, 1995).
acceptableAnswers: x^n + y^n = z^n has no positive-integer solutions for n > 2 (proved by Wiles, 1995).
